questions.q: What makes a priority queue different from an ordinary queue?
questions.explain: An ordinary queue is first in, first out. A priority queue returns the item with the best priority, whenever it was added. Whether it is sorted inside is an implementation detail; a heap is not.
options: It hands out the most important item first, not the oldest
It cannot grow after it is created

questions.q: A priority queue is an unsorted array: adding pushes to the end, taking scans for the most urgent job. What does draining n jobs cost?
questions.explain: Each take scans all remaining jobs: n − 1, then n − 2, and so on, about n²/2 comparisons in total. With 10,000 jobs that was about 50 million comparisons.

questions.q: If you keep the job array sorted instead, what gets slow?
questions.explain: A sorted array makes the take O(1) (it is at one end), but every insert has to shift elements to open a gap. A heap makes both operations O(log n).
options: Taking the most urgent job, which becomes O(n)
Adding a job, which must find its place and shift the others: O(n)
Nothing; a sorted array is always the best priority queue
Reading the size of the queue

questions.q: Which statement is guaranteed in a valid min-heap?
questions.explain: The heap property only relates parents to their children. Siblings can be in any order, and the maximum can be any leaf. That weaker rule is what makes a heap cheaper to maintain than a sorted structure.
options: The array is sorted in ascending order
Every left child is smaller than its right sibling
Every parent is less than or equal to each of its children
The largest item is the last element of the array

questions.q: These numbers were pushed into a min-heap. What does the internal array look like? (Push appends and sifts up.)
questions.explain: 4; 7 stays under 4; 2 swaps with 4 to the root; 9 stays under 7; 1 goes to index 4, swaps with 7 (index 1), then with 2 (index 0). The result 1 2 4 9 7 is a valid heap, but it is not sorted.

questions.q: Why must a binary heap be a complete tree?
questions.explain: A complete tree fills level by level from the left, which maps exactly onto consecutive array slots, and it has the smallest possible height. Both facts give O(log n) operations without any pointers.
options: So it can be stored in an array with no gaps and stays as short as possible, height ⌊log₂ n⌋
Because complete trees are binary search trees
So that equal items keep their order

questions.q: In the array layout, which indexes hold the children of the node at index 4?
questions.explain: Children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2: 9 and 10.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both children of a node share a parent: 1 and 2 → 0, 7 and 8 → 3, 13 → 6. The formula is the inverse of 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

questions.q: Why does pop move the last item into the root before sifting down?
questions.explain: Taking the root leaves a hole at the top. Filling it with the last item removes a slot from the end, so the shape stays complete; only the order needs repairing, which sift down does in O(log n).
options: Because the last item is always the largest
Removing the last slot is the only removal that keeps the tree complete
Because the last item is always a child of the root

questions.q: During sift down in a min-heap, both children are smaller than the item. What must you do?
questions.explain: The child that moves up becomes the parent of its sibling, so it must be the smaller one. Swapping with the larger child would put it above a smaller sibling and break the heap property.
options: Swap with the left child, always
Swap with the larger child, to keep the tree balanced
Stop, because the item is already in place

questions.q: This sift down has a bug: it always swaps with the left child. What does it print?
questions.explain: 9 swaps with 5 because it looks only left. Now 5 is the root but its right child 2 is smaller: the heap property is broken. Correct code picks the smaller child, 2, giving 2 5 9.

questions.q: A buggy pop always moves the last item to the root. What does it print for a heap with one item?
questions.explain: Popping the only item empties the array, then items[0] = last puts it straight back. The heap still reports one item that was already handed out. The correct code only moves last when the array is not empty after removing it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every pop returns the smallest item present at that moment: 1, then (after 2 and 3 arrive) 2, 3 and 4. The 5 stays inside. Pushes and pops can interleave freely.

questions.q: The lesson's Heap takes a before(a, b) function. How do you turn it into a max-heap of numbers?
questions.explain: before answers "should a come out before b?". For a max-heap, the larger one should. Note it must return a boolean: b - a is a sort comparator, and since every non-zero number is truthy, it would claim "before" in both directions for almost every pair.
options: Reverse the array after every push

questions.q: Four receipt emails with the same priority were queued in order 1, 2, 3, 4, but came out 4, 3, 1, 2. Why?
questions.explain: Equal items can move past each other during sifts. For a fair job queue, add a tie-breaker such as an increasing sequence number so no two jobs compare as equal.
options: The heap has a bug in sift up
Heaps are not stable: nothing in the heap property preserves the order of equal items
JavaScript compares objects by memory address
The emails were pushed in the wrong order

questions.q: Which before function gives a fair job queue (smaller priority first, older first among equals)?
questions.explain: Compare priority first, and only when priorities are equal fall back to the sequence number. <= alone does not make a heap stable, and the && version wrongly treats an urgent new job as not earlier than an old slow one.
options: (a, b) => a.priority < b.priority || (a.priority === b.priority && a.seq < b.seq)

questions.q: A job arrives with a missing priority. What does this print?
questions.explain: Any comparison with undefined (which becomes NaN) is false. The job is never "before" anything and nothing is "before" it, so it can sit anywhere and break the ordering around it. Validate priorities when jobs are added.

questions.q: You change the priority field of a job that is already inside the heap. What happens?
questions.explain: The heap only restores order during push and pop. Changing a field behind its back can leave a small value deep in the tree. Remove and re-add the job (with an index map), or push a new entry and skip the stale one later.
options: JavaScript throws, because heap items are frozen
Nothing moves, so the heap property may now be broken and pops can return the wrong job
The job moves to the end of the array

questions.q: Heapify sifts down every node that has children. Why does it go from the last such node back to the root?
questions.explain: Leaves are already heaps. Processing nodes from the bottom up means every node's children are roots of valid heaps when it is sifted, so one sift down fixes its whole subtree.
options: Because the root is the most important node
Sift down needs both subtrees below a node to already be heaps, and going backwards finishes them first

questions.q: What does heapify cost for n items, and why?
questions.explain: Half the nodes are leaves (no work), a quarter sift at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on. The total is less than n levels, so O(n), which is faster than n pushes at O(n log n) in the worst case.
options: O(n log n), because every node sifts down the full height
O(n), because most nodes are near the bottom and sift only a level or two
O(log n), because it only touches one path
O(n²), because it compares every pair

questions.q: Heapify starts at the last node that has children. Which index is that for these arrays?
questions.explain: Nodes from ⌊n / 2⌋ onwards are leaves. With 7 items, index 2 has children 5 and 6; with 10, index 4 has child 9. With a single item, −1 means the loop does not run at all: one item is already a heap.

questions.q: Which describes heap sort?
questions.explain: Heapify is O(n) and each of the n − 1 extractions sifts down O(log n), all inside the same array. Equal items can swap order, so it is not stable.
options: O(n²) worst case, stable, O(n) extra memory
O(n log n) worst case, not stable, O(1) extra memory
O(n) worst case, stable, O(1) extra memory
O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case, like quicksort

questions.q: To sort ascending in place, heap sort builds a max-heap. Why not a min-heap?
questions.explain: The sorted part grows from the back of the array. Swapping the maximum into the last free slot puts it in its final position; a min-heap would put the smallest item at the end, producing descending order.
options: Each step swaps the root to the end of the heap region; the largest item belongs at the end
Min-heaps cannot be built with heapify
It does not matter; both give ascending order in place

questions.q: What does the array look like after heapify (as a max-heap), before any extraction?
questions.explain: Index 1 (8) is sifted first: its children are 9 and 5, so 8 and 9 swap, giving 3 9 1 8 5. Then the root 3 swaps with 9, and again with 8: 9 8 1 3 5. Every parent is at least its children, but the array is not sorted.

questions.q: To keep the 10 highest-revenue products from a stream, which heap do you keep, and of what size?
questions.explain: You need quick access to the smallest of your current winners, because that is the one a newcomer must beat. A size-k min-heap gives it in O(1) and replaces it in O(log k).
options: A min-heap of size 10, whose root is the weakest of the current top 10

questions.q: Selecting the top k of n items with a size-k heap costs what, compared with sorting everything?
questions.explain: Each of the n items costs at most one O(log k) heap operation. With k = 5 and a million items that is far less than sorting a million, and only 5 items stay in memory, so it works on streams too.
options: O(k log n) vs O(n log n)
O(n log k) vs O(n log n), and the heap holds only k items

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: (A sorted array stands in for the heap here; only its front matters.) After 40, 10, 90 the smallest winner is 10. 20 beats 10; 70 beats 20; 60 beats 40. The survivors are the top three: 60, 70, 90, with the weakest at the front.

questions.q: You merge k sorted order logs with N entries in total using a heap of the current front items. What is the cost?
questions.explain: The heap never holds more than k items (one per list), and every one of the N entries is pushed and popped once: N × O(log k).

questions.q: What does this k-way merge print?
questions.explain: (A sorted array of fronts stands in for the heap.) The smallest front is taken each time, and it is replaced by the next item of the same list, so the output is fully sorted. A real heap makes each step O(log k) instead of a sort.

questions.q: Urgent jobs keep arriving all day, and a low-priority cleanup job never runs. What is this called, and what is a common fix?
questions.explain: A strict priority queue can postpone low-priority work forever. Aging, a guaranteed share of workers per priority, or a maximum wait all ensure every job eventually runs. A sequence number only orders equal priorities.
options: Starvation; aging, so a job's effective priority improves the longer it waits
A memory leak; use a WeakMap

questions.q: Your code treats priority 1 as most urgent. You move the jobs to a queue library where a higher priority number runs first. What happens if you keep your numbers?
questions.explain: Priority direction is a convention, and conventions differ (@zudojs/queue runs higher numbers first). Check it before setting priorities, and write a test that the most urgent job really comes out first.
options: The least important jobs run first

questions.q: Why do production job systems keep waiting jobs in a database or Redis rather than only in an in-memory heap?
questions.explain: Jobs are promises to do work later. They must survive restarts and be visible to every worker. Redis sorted sets offer the same O(log n) add and take-minimum operations, but durably and shared.
options: An in-memory heap is lost when the process crashes or restarts, and other worker processes cannot share it
Heaps only work for numbers below 2³²

questions.q: A customer cancels an order whose job is somewhere in the heap. How fast can a plain binary heap find that job?
questions.explain: A heap only knows where the minimum is. Finding anything else means scanning. Keep a Map from job to index (updated on every swap) or mark it cancelled and skip it when it is popped.
options: O(log n), by walking down from the root
O(n), because the heap has no search order
It cannot be found at all

questions.q: Finish push(items, value) for a min-heap stored in an array: append, then sift up. It should print 1 3 2 7 4 5.
questions.explain: The new item starts in the last slot and swaps with its parent while it is smaller. It stops at the root or as soon as the parent is not larger: at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ swaps.

questions.q: Finish pop(items) for a min-heap array: return the root (or undefined when empty), move the last item to the root and sift it down, swapping with the smaller child. It should print 1 2 3 5 8 9 undefined.
questions.explain: Handle the empty heap first, then the one-item case (only move last to the root when something is left). Sift down swaps with the smaller child until neither child is smaller. Popping everything returns the items in ascending order, and the seventh pop finds the heap empty.

questions.q: Finish before(a, b) for a fair job queue: smaller priority first, and among equal priorities, smaller seq first. The heap and the jobs are given. It should print the four jobs in fair order.
questions.explain: Priority decides first; the sequence number only breaks ties. Because no two jobs compare equal any more, the heap's instability cannot reorder the emails.
questions.expected: payment, email A, email B, email C, sitemap

questions.q: Six couriers quoted a delivery price. Finish cheapest(quotes, k): return the k cheapest quotes, cheapest first, keeping at most k quotes at a time in a max-heap (the MaxHeap class is given). It should print 1800 2100 2500.
questions.explain: This is top-k mirrored: to keep the k smallest, use a max-heap, whose root is the most expensive of the current winners, the one a cheaper quote replaces. Popping gives most expensive first, so reverse at the end.

questions.q: Finish heapify(items): turn the array into a min-heap in place in O(n), by sifting down every node that has children, from the last one back to the root. The siftDown helper is given. It should print 1 2 4 5 3 6 true.
questions.explain: Index 2 is the last node with a child (index 5). Sifting 2, 1 and 0 in that order means each node's subtrees are already heaps when it is processed. The last check tests the heap property directly.

questions.q: Order totals arrive one at a time. Finish add(total) so that third() always returns the 3rd largest total seen so far (or undefined until there are three), using a size-3 min-heap. A tiny min-heap is given. It should print undefined undefined 5000 7000 7000 9000.
questions.explain: The heap holds the three largest totals so far; its root is the smallest of them, which is exactly the 3rd largest overall. Each new total costs O(log 3), effectively O(1), however long the stream runs.

questions.q: Cancelled jobs are not removed from the heap; they are skipped when popped (lazy deletion). What does this print?
questions.explain: B has the best priority, but when it reaches the root it is popped and skipped, and next keeps going. Cancelling is O(1); the cost is paid later, O(log n) per skipped entry, and the heap holds stale entries until then.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The class is named MinHeap, but the before function makes it a max-heap: larger comes first. The first pop returns 980,000; after the two pushes the largest is 2,300,000. Three items remain: 12,500, 45,000 and 7,800.

questions.q: Finish merge(lists): combine sorted arrays of order numbers into one sorted array using the given heap, holding at most one entry per list at a time. It should print 1001 1002 1003 1004 1006 1007 1009.
questions.explain: Seed the heap with the first item of every non-empty list. Each pop outputs the smallest front and replaces it with the next item from the same list, so the heap never holds more than k entries: O(N log k). The empty list is skipped when seeding.

questions.q: Finish heapSort(a) so it sorts ascending in place: heapify as a max-heap with the given siftDown(a, i, n), then repeatedly swap the root to the end of the heap region and sift down within the smaller heap. It should print 1200 1200 3500 15000 45000 89000.
questions.explain: Heapify is O(n); each of the n − 1 swaps is followed by an O(log n) sift down limited to the unsorted front part (n = end). Total O(n log n), with no extra array.
